title: Wide-field calcium imaging of cortex-wide activity in awake, head-fixed mice
author: Ren, Komiyama
materials: Dental acrylic cement (Contemporary Ortho-Jet™ Powder and Jet Liquid)
Fiber optic light source with gooseneck (KL 1500 LED)
Mouse gas anesthesia head holder (nose cone and bite bar)
Timing: ∼24 h/1-h continuous imaging at 30 Hz

steps.title: Sterilize workspace and tools
steps.instruction: Sterilize the surface of the surgery table with chlorhexidine solution; sterilize scalpel, scissors, forceps, double‑end carver, and the custom stainless‑steel headbar using a hot‑bead sterilizer.

steps.title: Prepare gel foam pieces
steps.instruction: Cut sterile gel foam (Ethicon 1975) into ~1 × 1 mm pieces; use dry pieces unless the specific foam requires saline moisturisation—if so, soak the pieces in saline before use.

steps.title: Activate heating pad
steps.instruction: Turn on the servo‑controlled heating pad and set it to maintain the mouse body temperature at 35 °C–37 °C throughout surgery.

steps.title: Anesthetize and ventilate mouse
steps.instruction: Induce anesthesia in an adult mouse (6 weeks–4 months, either sex) with 3 % isoflurane in 100 % O₂ in an induction box; transfer the mouse to a nose‑cone ventilator, adjust isoflurane to 1–1.5 % in 100 % O₂ to keep breathing at ~1 breath s⁻¹, place the mouse on the heating pad and continuously monitor respiration.

steps.title: Protect the eyes
steps.instruction: Apply a generous amount of Vaseline to both eyes to prevent drying and exposure to irritants during the procedure.

steps.title: Clean and antisepticise area
steps.instruction: Wipe the surgical region 2–3 times with cotton swabs soaked in 70 % ethanol, then wipe until fully infiltrated with betadine.

steps.title: Incise scalp and expose skull
steps.instruction: Using fine scissors, make a ~2 mm incision between the ears, cut a circular piece of scalp to expose the dorsal cortex and cerebellum, and retract the remaining scalp with forceps; remove any interfering hair.

steps.title: Remove periosteum and control bleeding
steps.instruction: Gently scrape off the periosteum with a scalpel; if bleeding occurs, press with a dry cotton swab until it stops (usually ≤5 min, abort if >10 min), rinse the skull with saline several times to clear bloodstains.

steps.title: Detach occipital muscles and insert gel foam
steps.instruction: Using a scalpel, detach muscles from the occipital bone and push them aside; insert small gel‑foam pieces into the gaps to stop bleeding (dry foam preferred). If bleeding persists, press with dry cotton swabs and rinse; abort if bleeding continues >20 min.

steps.title: Clean skull surface
steps.instruction: Wipe the skull with cotton swabs soaked in 3 % hydrogen peroxide to remove remaining soft tissue.

steps.title: Dry skull
steps.instruction: Allow the dorsal skull to air‑dry for ~5 min until it appears whiter and less transparent; if drying is slow, gently blow with a compressed‑air duster (avoid strong airflow).

steps.title: Apply cyanoacrylate and acrylic over occipital region
steps.instruction: Remove any remaining gel foam, apply small drops of cyanoacrylate glue to cover muscles and occipital bone, let cure; then add drops of dental acrylic cement with a double‑end carver to build a thick layer, let cure; finally apply cyanoacrylate with the carver to cover the skin along the cuts.

steps.title: Implant headbar
steps.instruction: Apply a small amount of cyanoacrylate glue to the interparietal bone, place the custom headbar 0.5–1 mm posterior to lambda, eyeball‑adjust its angle until parallel to the skull’s transverse plane, and hold until steady.

steps.title: Secure headbar with glue and acrylic
steps.instruction: Add cyanoacrylate drops through the headbar holes to create a glue layer between headbar and cement, let cure; then apply dental acrylic cement around the headbar to embed its middle part and cover bones posterior to lambda, let cure.

steps.title: Build transparent glue layers on skull
steps.instruction: Apply a thin layer of cyanoacrylate glue over the dorsal cortex using a double‑end carver, spread evenly, and allow to cure (~5 min).

substeps.instruction: Repeat the application 3–4 times; the skull becomes increasingly transparent and blood vessels become visible within ~20 min.
If bleeding starts after glue application, carefully drill off the cured glue with a dental drill, pause every 30 s to cool, blow debris with compressed air, and reapply glue.

steps.title: Shield eyes from excitation light
steps.instruction: Cut a ~5 mm length of black heat‑shrink tubing (≈2 cm diameter), glue it around the skull circumference, then fill the gap with black dental acrylic cement; after curing, optionally cover the cement with black electrical tape or paint with black marker. Avoid cement flow onto the transparent glue layer.

steps.title: Administer analgesia and antibiotics
steps.instruction: Inject Buprenorphine subcutaneously at 0.1 mg kg⁻¹ body weight and Baytril at 10 mg kg⁻¹ body weight.

steps.title: Recover mouse and monitor preparation
steps.instruction: After the dental acrylic in step 16 has cured, remove the mouse from the nose cone, place it in a recovery cage, and monitor until fully awake; periodically inspect the skull window for clarity. If cloudiness or yellowing appears, inject Baytril (10 mg kg⁻¹) plus Dexamethasone (1 mg kg⁻¹) subcutaneously for 3–5 consecutive days; discontinue the experiment if infection persists.

steps.title: Transform imaging data for PCA
steps.instruction: Convert the 3‑D Δf/f image stack (row × column × frame) into a 2‑D matrix (pixel × frame) to prepare for principal component analysis.

steps.title: Perform PCA and retain components
steps.instruction: Run PCA on the matrix, treating pixels as variables and frames as observations; retain the first 40 principal components that explain ~95 % of total variance (30–50 PCs often capture >90 % variance).

steps.title: Run ICA on retained PCs
steps.instruction: Feed the retained PCs into the JADER ICA algorithm to extract 40 independent components (ICs), each representing a spatial mode.

steps.title: Identify and exclude artifact ICs
steps.instruction: Visually inspect the IC spatial maps, label those corresponding to hemodynamic or other artifacts, and exclude them from further reconstruction.

steps.title: Reconstruct cleaned Δf/f images
steps.instruction: Multiply the remaining ICs by their time series, sum the products, and then add back the original per‑pixel mean that was subtracted during PCA to obtain the final artifact‑reduced image stack.

description: Wide-field calcium imaging with genetically encoded calcium indicators, especially the GCaMP family, has become an attractive approach to visualize the cortex-wide neural activity in living mice under various sensory and cognitive processes (Cardin et al., 2020; Ren and Komiyama, 2021). It provides a good spatiotemporal resolution by simultaneous illumination of large cortical areas and a high signal-to-noise ratio from bright GCaMP fluorescence. Genetic encoding of GCaMP also enables stable expression for longitudinal recordings and probing specific neuronal populations through genetically restricted expression. The protocol below describes the specific steps for using wide-field calcium imaging to monitor the cortex-wide activity in transgenic mice expressing GCaMP6s widely in cortical excitatory neurons. However, this protocol can also be used to image the cortex-wide activity in specific neuronal populations, such as neurons in specific cortical layers (Gilad et al., 2018; Valley et al., 2020) and different subtypes of cortical inhibitory neurons (Allen et al., 2017). Furthermore, this protocol can be adapted to image the cortex-wide fluorescence signals from other genetically encoded indicators, such as indicators for neurotransmitters (Lohani et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2016). In addition, this protocol can also be incorporated with other recording modalities, such as electrophysiological recordings, to simultaneously record from the cortex and deep brain regions (Liu et al., 2021; Peters et al., 2021). Therefore, this protocol has a broad application to study different macroscopic properties of brain functions. The readers are encouraged to reference a recent protocol paper of similar experiments (Couto et al., 2021). It should be noted that this protocol, together with any modifications, should be approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) before implementation.
